## Frequently Asked Questions

**Is Korean skincare cheap because the ingredients are lower quality?**

No. The low prices come from market structure rather than formulation shortcuts. Intense domestic competition, shared manufacturing infrastructure through large contract manufacturers, short distribution chains, and lower marketing overhead all push the final price down without changing what goes in the bottle. Many inexpensive Korean products are developed at the same contract manufacturers that produce for global luxury brands.

**Why is Korean skincare cheaper than American skincare?**

The biggest differences are distribution and marketing. American brands often sell through a distributor and then a retailer, with each adding margin, and legacy brands carry substantial advertising costs in their pricing. Korean brands more often sell direct or through a single dominant domestic retailer, and grew largely through creators and reviews. Manufacturing scale through contract manufacturers also spreads R&D cost across many brands rather than one.

**If it is so cheap in Korea, why did I pay a lot for it in the US?**

Because the price you paid reflects the import chain rather than the Korean retail price. Freight, customs handling, distributor margin, and US retailer margin all stack on top of the original price. Our companion article on US K-beauty pricing breaks down where each layer goes.

**Does a cheap Korean product mean it is fake?**

Not on its own. Low prices are normal in this category. What is worth questioning is a price far below every other seller of the same item, which is a common counterfeit signal, especially on viral products from third party marketplace sellers. Check the manufacturing date, confirm the seller is authorized by the brand, and compare packaging against the brand's Korean site.

**Are Korean products sold in the US the same formula as in Korea?**

Usually, but not always. Some products are reformulated for the US market because certain UV filters approved in Korea are not approved by the FDA, which particularly affects sunscreens. If formulation matters to you, compare the ingredient lists rather than assuming the SKU is identical.

## Quick Answer: What cleanser should oily, sensitive, acne-prone skin use?

Skip the foaming "oil control" cleansers that leave you tight and squeaky, that tight feeling is barrier damage, and it makes oily, breakout-prone skin worse, not better. Go for a low-pH, fragrance-free cleanser (a gel or gentle milk) that removes oil and sunscreen without stripping. If you wear SPF or makeup, do a low-irritation first cleanse (micellar water or a cleansing milk) before it.

## Why Oily Skin Still Breaks Out From Harsh Cleansers

Let's clear up the myth first. Stripping your skin does not reduce oil. High-pH foaming cleansers (think old-school bar soaps and a lot of "acne wash" foams) blow past your skin's natural pH of around 4.7–5.5. When your barrier gets disrupted, two things happen: it loses water and gets irritated (the tingling and tightness), and your oil glands can actually ramp UP to compensate. So you end up oilier, more reactive, and with more clogged pores. Classic.

For acne-prone skin specifically, an impaired barrier is a bigger deal than most people realize. When the barrier is compromised, it's easier for irritation and inflammation to snowball, and inflammation is a huge driver of breakouts. So a cleanser that's "tough on oil" often makes the acne worse through the back door.

The other piece: fragrance and essential oils. Sensitive skin reacts to added fragrance more than any other ingredient category, and a shocking number of cleansers marketed as "gentle" still have it. When you can't read a Korean label, this is exactly the kind of thing that trips people up, the word "soothing" on the front tells you nothing about what's actually in the bottle. Yeah, K-beauty labels are impossible when you can't read Korean, which is half the reason picking the wrong product is so easy.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### Is foam or gel cleanser better for oily sensitive skin?
A low-pH gel is usually the safer bet. Many foaming cleansers rely on harsher surfactants and a higher pH to get that big lather, which is what leaves sensitive skin tight and reactive. There are gentle low-pH foams out there, but you have to check the formula, the foam-vs-gel label alone doesn't tell you whether it's stripping.

### Should I double cleanse if I have oily acne-prone skin?
Only when you're removing sunscreen or makeup. On those days, a gentle first cleanse (micellar water or a cleansing milk) followed by a low-pH water-based wash removes everything without scrubbing. On bare-face nights, one gentle cleanse is plenty, double cleansing every time can over-strip and backfire.

### Why does my oily skin still feel dry and tight after washing?
Because the cleanser is disrupting your barrier. Tightness after cleansing means the product stripped away too much of your natural lipids, often from a high pH or harsh surfactants. Switching to a low-pH, fragrance-free cleanser and following with a hydrating toner usually fixes it fast.

### Do I need a separate exfoliating cleanser for clogged pores?
No, and it's often better not to. Combining exfoliation into your daily cleanser means you can't control the frequency, which is risky for sensitive skin. Keep your cleanser gentle and handle exfoliation (a BHA, or a mild physical/clay cleanser a couple times a week) as a separate, controllable step.

### Are Korean cleansers good for sensitive acne-prone skin?
Many are, because low-pH, fragrance-free, centella-based formulas are common in K-beauty. But "gentle" on the front of a Korean label doesn't guarantee it's fragrance-free or low-pH, you have to check the actual ingredient list, which is hard when it's printed in Korean.

## Quick Answer: Why Does My Skincare Keep Making My Skin Worse?

**When skincare progressively makes your skin worse, it's almost always a damaged moisture barrier, usually from too many actives, over-exfoliation, or fragrance/essential oil irritation stacking up over time.** The counterintuitive fix isn't adding a repair product on top of everything. It's stripping your routine back to a gentle cleanser, one hydrating layer, and moisturizer for two to three weeks so your skin can actually heal.

## The Situation You're In

You started with good intentions. Maybe a vitamin C in the morning, an exfoliating acid a few nights a week, retinol on the others, an essence, a couple of serums, that trending ampoule everyone on TikTok swears by. For a while it felt productive. Then your skin started getting… weird. Tight after cleansing. Stinging when you apply things that never used to sting. Little rough bumps. Redness that comes and goes. Dryness that sits *under* the surface no matter how much moisturizer you pile on.

So you did the logical thing: you added more. A richer cream. A soothing serum. Another mask. And somehow it got *worse*. Now you're looking in the mirror feeling like your skin is actively working against you, and every new product is a gamble you can't afford to keep losing.

Here's the reframe: your skin isn't rejecting skincare. It's overwhelmed by it.

## Why This Happens

Your moisture barrier is the outermost layer of your skin, the thing that holds water in and keeps irritants out. When it's healthy, products absorb nicely and your skin feels calm. When it's compromised, everything changes. Water evaporates out faster than you can replace it (that's the dryness that moisturizer doesn't fix), and irritants get in more easily (that's the new stinging and redness).

The thing is, a stripped barrier doesn't announce itself as "barrier damage." It shows up as symptoms that look like they need *more* treatment, dryness that reads as "I need more moisture," bumps that read as "I need to exfoliate," dullness that reads as "I need actives." So you keep feeding the fire. Over-exfoliation is the biggest culprit I see: acids plus retinol plus a scrub plus a "brightening" toner that quietly has more acid in it. It adds up faster than anyone expects.

Fragrance and essential oils are the other quiet saboteurs. A lot of gorgeous-smelling K-beauty is loaded with them, and on a healthy barrier you might never notice. On a compromised one, they're a daily low-grade irritant keeping you stuck in the red zone. And silent reformulations don't help, the product you loved a year ago may have changed, which is exactly the kind of thing worth checking when your holy grail suddenly turns on you. ### 3. Seal it in, and don't overthink the moisturizer

- **Worse-with-more-products almost always means barrier damage**, not a missing step.
- **Over-exfoliation and fragrance/essential oils** are the two most common causes, count how many acids and actives are quietly stacked in your routine.
- **The fix is subtraction:** gentle cleanser, hydrating toner, moisturizer, sunscreen, for 2–3 weeks.
- **Reintroduce actives one at a time** after your skin calms down.
- **Check whether a beloved product silently reformulated** if it suddenly started irritating you.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### How do I know if my skin barrier is damaged or if it's just purging?

Purging is temporary, happens only when you start an ingredient that speeds up cell turnover (retinoids, AHAs/BHAs), and shows up as breakouts in your usual breakout areas that clear within about 4–6 weeks. Barrier damage shows up as stinging, redness, tight dryness, rough texture, and reactivity to products that never bothered you before, and it doesn't resolve on its own, it needs you to back off. If you're stinging and not just breaking out, treat it as a barrier issue.

### How long does it take to repair a skin barrier?

For most people, a mild-to-moderate barrier reset takes about two to three weeks of a stripped-back gentle routine before things feel calm again. More significant damage can take a month or more. The non-negotiable part is *stopping the irritants*, no acids, no retinol, no fragrance, because the barrier can't rebuild while it's still being disrupted daily.

### Can I keep using vitamin C or retinol during a barrier reset?

Not while you're actively resetting. Both are worth having in a healthy routine, but during a reset they're exactly the kind of active that keeps your skin from calming down. Pause everything, get your skin comfortable, then reintroduce one active at a time with a couple of weeks between each so you can tell what's actually working versus what's irritating.

### Is fragrance really that bad for my skin?

Not for everyone, and not always, plenty of people use fragranced products with zero problems. But on a compromised or reactive barrier, fragrance and essential oils are a common low-grade irritant that keeps you stuck. During a reset specifically, going fragrance-free removes a variable so you can actually see what your skin does without it.

## The Bottom Line

If your skin has been getting progressively worse, the most useful thing you can do isn't buy a new product, it's take things away. Strip back to gentle cleanser, hydration, moisturizer, and sunscreen, hold there until your skin is genuinely calm, and reintroduce actives slowly. Your barrier does the healing; your job is to stop getting in its way.

## Quick Answer: Why Is PDRN So Popular Right Now?

PDRN blew up because it sits at the intersection of two things Gen Z loves: a slightly sci-fi backstory (it's derived from salmon DNA) and a plausible-sounding "repair and regenerate" promise. It got huge in Korea through in-clinic "salmon DNA" injectables first, then trickled into at-home serums, and now TikTok runs on the before-and-after glow content. The hype is real, but it's doing a lot of borrowing from the injectable version, which is not the same thing as the serum on your shelf.

## The Situation You're In

You've seen "PDRN" slapped across what feels like every new Korean serum launch this year, and the comments are all some version of *this changed my skin*. You're ingredient-literate enough to be suspicious of anything trending this hard, but also curious enough that you've got a tab open on a product page right now. The thing you can't get a straight answer on: is PDRN actually doing something, or is it the latest word brands print on the box because it tests well on your generation?

Fair instinct. Let's check the actual science and the actual ingredient list before you commit.

## What PDRN Actually Is (And What It Isn't)

PDRN stands for polydeoxyribonucleotide, basically fragments of DNA, usually extracted and purified from salmon sperm or roe. The idea is that these DNA fragments are structurally similar enough to human DNA to interact with your skin's repair pathways, nudging cell turnover and supporting the skin's own regeneration. In a medical setting, PDRN has genuine research behind it for wound healing and tissue repair, which is where a lot of the credibility comes from.

Here's the part the marketing skips: **"salmon DNA" and "PDRN" are not interchangeable terms**, even though brands use them like they are. PDRN is a specific, purified, fragmented form. Most "PDRN" serums actually list Sodium DNA on the label and let you assume it's the same ingredient from the injectable studies. It often isn't, or it's there in amounts that make the label true but the effect modest. I went deep on this exact distinction in [What Is PDRN Skincare, Really?](https://www.seoulsister.com/blog/what-is-pdrn-skincare-really-why-salmon-dna-and-pdrn-are) because it's the single most misunderstood thing about this ingredient.

The other reality check: most of the impressive PDRN research is on **injectable** PDRN delivered into the skin by a needle. A topical serum has to get the molecule through your stratum corneum, which DNA fragments are not naturally great at. So a serum can be worth using, it's generally soothing, hydrating, and barrier-friendly, but it's not going to replicate an in-clinic treatment. Anyone implying otherwise is selling you the injectable's reputation at serum prices.

## Why It Got So Popular So Fast

A few things stacked up at once. First, Korea's clinic culture normalized "salmon DNA" treatments years before the serums existed, so there was already a built-in association with glassy, recovered-looking skin. When the at-home versions launched, they inherited that halo for free.

Second, PDRN slots neatly into the *barrier repair* and *skin regeneration* conversation that's been dominating K-beauty since the whole "slugging" and "skin cycling" wave. People who overdid actives and wrecked their barriers were primed for anything that promised recovery and calm. PDRN markets itself right into that gap.

Third, and this is the honest part, it's a *great word*. "Polydeoxyribonucleotide derived from salmon DNA" sounds like a lab breakthrough. It's genuinely more interesting content than "here's some niacinamide." The sponsored-influencer cycle loves a novel-sounding hero ingredient, and PDRN gives them one. That doesn't make it fake. It just means the volume of hype is outrunning the strength of the topical evidence, and those are two different things to keep separate.

## What Actually Works: How to Buy PDRN Without Getting Played

**Read the ingredient list, not the front of the box.** In Seoul Sister's database, of 188 products with "PDRN" in the name and a complete ingredient record, 171 list Sodium DNA and zero list polydeoxyribonucleotide (counted October 2026). So the ingredient you're most likely buying is Sodium DNA. That isn't a bad ingredient, but it isn't PDRN, and it shouldn't be priced like the injectable. When the list isn't in English, the Seoul Sister [ingredient encyclopedia](https://www.seoulsister.com/ingredients) and [product database](https://www.seoulsister.com/products) are there precisely so you can check what's actually in it instead of trusting the marketing render.

**Treat PDRN as a supporting player, not your whole routine.** The skin it genuinely helps is skin that's irritated, over-exfoliated, or just dull and dehydrated. If that's you, the smarter move is to get your barrier calm *first*, then let a PDRN serum ride on top. A plain, well-formulated hydrating base does more heavy lifting than people admit, something like the [Klairs Supple Preparation Unscented Toner](https://www.seoulsister.com/products/f60cfa78-383b-4a94-b117-b7b3799987eb), which is built on betaine and [centella asiatica](https://www.seoulsister.com/ingredients/centella-asiatica-extract), with [sodium hyaluronate](https://www.seoulsister.com/ingredients/sodium-hyaluronate) further down and no fragrance or essential oils, gives PDRN a calm, hydrated canvas to work on. Unglamorous, but it's the step that actually moves the needle.

**Don't layer it over a stripped, angry barrier.** PDRN serums are usually gentle, but if your skin is already reactive, start with how you cleanse. A non-stripping cleanse keeps your barrier intact so you're not fighting uphill. ## Key Takeaways

- **PDRN is real, but the serum isn't the injectable.** Most strong evidence is for in-clinic PDRN delivered by needle; topical serums are generally soothing and barrier-friendly, not miracle regenerators.
- **"Salmon DNA" and Sodium DNA are not purified PDRN.** In Seoul Sister's catalog, 171 of 188 "PDRN" products list Sodium DNA and none list polydeoxyribonucleotide.
- **It got popular from clinic culture + the barrier-repair trend + a genuinely cool-sounding name**, not necessarily from topical results outperforming everything else.
- **It works best as a supporting step** on calm, hydrated skin, not as a rescue for a wrecked barrier.
- **SPF and a non-stripping routine matter more** than any single trending active.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### Does topical PDRN actually work, or do you need injections?
Topical PDRN serums can genuinely soothe, hydrate, and support a stressed barrier, and plenty of people love how their skin feels using them. But the dramatic "regeneration" research you've seen is mostly on injectable PDRN that gets delivered past the skin's surface barrier. Treat a serum as a nice supporting step, not a needle-free version of the clinic treatment.

### Is PDRN safe if I'm allergic to fish?
This is worth flagging to a doctor if you have a known fish or shellfish allergy, since PDRN is derived from salmon. The ingredient is highly purified, but "highly purified" isn't a guarantee, patch test, and when in doubt check with an allergist before committing to daily use.

### What's the difference between PDRN and PN in skincare?
PN (polynucleotides) are longer-chain versions of the same family, while PDRN is the more fragmented form. Brands often use them in overlapping marketing, and both ride the same "salmon DNA repair" story. For a topical serum, the more important question isn't PDRN-vs-PN, it's which ingredient is actually on the label (usually Sodium DNA) and where it sits in the list, which tells you more honestly than the buzzword on the front.

### Can I use PDRN with retinol or exfoliating acids?
Generally yes, PDRN's calming, barrier-supporting profile actually pairs nicely with the irritation potential of actives. A common approach is using actives on their own nights and letting PDRN support recovery. If you're layering several strong things and not sure about the order, that's exactly the kind of thing worth double-checking for your specific routine.

### Is PDRN worth the money or is it overhyped?
Both. It's a legitimately decent soothing/hydrating ingredient, so it's not a scam, but the price premium often reflects the buzzword more than the dose. Worth it if you check where Sodium DNA sits on the ingredient list and the price matches; a waste if you're paying hero-ingredient prices for a trace amount under a "salmon DNA" sticker.

## The Bottom Line

PDRN isn't hype with nothing behind it, there's real science, it's just mostly about the injectable version, and the serum on your shelf is a gentler, more modest relative riding that reputation. The move isn't to avoid it; it's to buy it with your eyes open, check where the actual ingredient sits on the list, and keep your barrier and SPF handled so you're not building a regeneration routine on sand.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### How often should I use a Korean face mask?

A mask is an occasional boost, not a daily essential, so most people do fine with a sheet mask once or twice a week and a wash-off clay mask once or twice a week at most. Clay masks on oily skin shouldn't be stacked back to back, and you shouldn't use any mask on skin that's broken, burning, or actively irritated. If a rash is spreading or your skin is burning, see a doctor rather than reaching for a mask.

### Does "cica" or "calming" on the front mean a mask is fragrance-free?

No. In Seoul Sister's catalog, 33% of masks list fragrance or parfum outright, and that climbs to 62% once you count essential oils and fragrance allergens like limonene, linalool, and citral. The word on the front is marketing, so the only way to know is to read the ingredient list and scan for those terms yourself.

### Can a face mask replace my moisturizer or sunscreen?

No, a mask is a short, occasional top-up on an existing routine, not a replacement for either. Sheet and overnight masks deliver a burst of humectants, but you still want your regular moisturizer to seal that in and daily sunscreen for actual protection. If you need a daily moisturizer to pair with these, start with our [8 Korean moisturizer picks by skin type](https://www.seoulsister.com/blog/best-korean-moisturizer-for-your-skin-type-8-picks-for-dry).

### Why is water the first ingredient on most sheet masks?

Because 78% of the sheet masks in Seoul Sister's catalog list water first, which just means the serum is mostly water plus humectants. That's normal and not a red flag. The ingredients that make one mask meaningfully different, like centella, ceramides, or hyaluronic acid, sit a few lines below the first, so that's where to look when you compare two masks.

### Are sheet masks or clay masks better for oily skin?

For oily or congested pores, a wash-off kaolin clay mask like the SKIN1004 Madagascar Centella clay stick or the Isntree Mugwort Calming Clay is usually the better fit, used once or twice a week. Clay absorbs excess surface oil; a hydrating sheet mask doesn't do that job. That said, oily skin that's also dehydrated can use both on different days.

### What ingredients should a Korean lip balm have for dry, chapped lips?

Look for sealing ingredients like shea butter, squalane, waxes, petrolatum or plant oils to slow water loss, ideally paired with a ceramide for the barrier. ### Are Korean lip sleeping masks worth it, or is a regular balm enough?

A sleeping mask is worth it specifically if your lips crack overnight, because it's thicker and gets undisturbed hours to seal while you sleep. Often it's something else in your day undoing the balm, like a scented lip product, a flavored or SLS toothpaste, constant lip-licking, or a retinoid creeping onto the lip line. ## Quick Answer

**Question:** What does a comedogenic rating actually tell you, and can you trust it?

**Answer:** A comedogenic rating is a 0-to-5 score most lists trace back to a 1989 study where ingredients were applied to the inside of rabbit ears, not human skin. A high number is a reason to pay attention, not proof a product will clog your pores, and a low number is not a guarantee either. The most reliable test is reading the full label and watching your own skin over several weeks.

---

## The Situation You're In

You searched a comedogenic rating because something gave you small bumps, or you're holding a product you want to buy and you're trying not to repeat a mistake. You found a chart with tidy numbers next to ingredient names, and now you're trying to figure out whether that 4 next to one of your ingredients actually means anything.

Here's a quick thing you can do right now: flip your product over and read the back label, not the claims on the front. See if you can spot where an ingredient sits in the order, because that matters more than you'd think, and I'll explain why below.

---

## Why This Happens

The comedogenic scale feels scientific because it's a number, and numbers feel like answers. The 0-to-5 grades most online lists use come from a 1989 study by James Fulton, published in the Journal of the Society of Cosmetic Chemists. Each ingredient was applied to the inside of a rabbit's ear at 10% strength, five days a week for two weeks, then graded on how badly the follicles plugged up. That's where your chart comes from.

The problem is what the chart leaves out. Fulton himself wrote that the rabbit ear is extremely sensitive and that not everything which reacts on it will react on human skin. So the test was useful for flagging suspects, not for predicting your face. Later work complicated it further: a small 2006 study by Draelos and DiNardo in the Journal of the American Academy of Dermatology tested finished products containing high-rated ingredients on actual people (only six of them) and found they weren't necessarily comedogenic. Fulton himself did not accept that a lower concentration makes a high-rated ingredient safe, so the honest reading cuts both ways: a high rating is a reason to pay attention, and a low one is not a guarantee.

And then there's the telephone-game problem. A lot of comedogenic lists online repeat values that aren't even in Fulton's original table. The classic example: coconut oil gets passed around as "a 4 from Fulton," but Fulton's table lists coconut butter, not coconut oil. So some of the scary numbers people cite were never measured the way the chart implies. This is exactly the kind of thing we run into constantly at Seoul Sister when we cross-check what's actually printed on a label against what the internet claims about it.

## What Actually Works

The honest move is to stop treating the rating as a verdict and start using it as a starting point, then let your own skin be the final test. Here's the method.

**Read the full ingredient list on the back, and pay attention to order.** The claims on the front ("pore-friendly," "lightweight," even "non-comedogenic") tell you less than the actual list. On a US cosmetic, ingredients above 1% are listed from most to least, so an ingredient near the top carries more weight than one near the very end. One exception: if the product is a US acne treatment with a "Drug Facts" panel, its inactive ingredients are listed alphabetically, so order tells you nothing there.

**Know the handful of ingredients Fulton graded highest, as a watchlist, not a blacklist.** The six that Fulton graded 4 or 5 in his 1989 rabbit-ear test are isopropyl myristate (5), myristyl myristate (5), laureth-4 (5), isopropyl palmitate (4), ethylhexyl palmitate (4), and isostearyl isostearate (4). Seeing one high on a list is a reason to watch how your skin responds, not a reason to toss the product. For contrast, Fulton graded squalane a 1 and dimethicone a 1, both of which show up constantly in Korean skincare. You can read the full breakdown on our pages for [isopropyl palmitate](https://www.seoulsister.com/ingredients/isopropyl-palmitate), [squalane](https://www.seoulsister.com/ingredients/squalane), and [dimethicone](https://www.seoulsister.com/ingredients/dimethicone). Knowing the six is a starting point, not a complete list.

**Use format as a clue, not a rule.** As of November 2026, across Seoul Sister's catalog of 5,240 Korean skincare products with ingredient lists, about 9% list at least one of those six ingredients (488 products). That share isn't even across categories. Sun sticks list one about half the time (36 of 72), while other sunscreen formats like creams and cushions sit around 6% (35 of 544). Cleansing oils and balms land at 57% (120 of 210), lip care around 23%, and toners under 2%. To be clear, those are counts of what's printed on labels, not breakout rates on anyone's face. But if you suspect a sunscreen and it happens to be a stick, the format is worth knowing, because sticks list these far more often than other formats do.

**Change one thing at a time and give it real time.** Reactions can take weeks to months to show up on human skin, so a product isn't "safe" just because nothing happened in the first week. Introduce one new product, wait several weeks, and keep a simple note of what you started and when. If new small bumps appeared after starting something, the newest product is the first suspect. The exception: if the newest thing is an acne treatment like a retinoid or benzoyl peroxide and you were told to expect an adjustment period, check with the pharmacist or doctor who recommended it before stopping. If you want to understand why order and timing matter so much when a routine goes sideways, [this walkthrough on why skincare keeps making skin worse](https://www.seoulsister.com/blog/why-does-my-skincare-keep-making-my-skin-worse) goes deeper, and if you're not sure whether those bumps are even breakouts, [sebaceous filaments versus blackheads](https://www.seoulsister.com/blog/sebaceous-filaments-vs-blackheads-how-to-tell-treat) is worth a read before you blame an ingredient.

One more thing worth knowing: a product reformulating silently can undo all of this. The version you've used happily for a year can change, and the change is not always obvious from the front of the box, which is its own rabbit hole, covered in [why the same brand's similar product can wreck your skin](https://www.seoulsister.com/blog/same-brand-different-formula-why-that-similar-k-beauty-product-just-wrecked-your-skin).

## Frequently Asked Questions

### What does comedogenic rating mean?

A comedogenic rating is a 0-to-5 score estimating how likely an ingredient is to clog pores, and the grades most lists use come from James Fulton's 1989 study where ingredients were tested on the inside of rabbit ears at 10% strength. A higher number meant more severe follicle plugging in that test. It's a flag for attention, not a measurement of what will happen on your skin.

### Is a comedogenic rating of 2 bad?

A rating of 2 is not inherently bad, and the number alone can't tell you whether a product will clog your pores. Fulton's own test was done on highly sensitive rabbit ears, and he noted that not everything reacting there reacts on human skin. A mid-range rating is a reason to watch your skin, not a reason to avoid a product outright.

### Does non-comedogenic mean it won't clog pores?

No, "non-comedogenic" doesn't guarantee a product won't clog your pores. In the US it's a marketing claim; the FDA keeps no list of approved cosmetic claims, so these terms only have to be truthful and not misleading rather than meeting a defined standard. The American Academy of Dermatology still advises people with acne to choose products labeled "non-comedogenic" or "won't clog pores" as a reasonable starting point, but your own skin over several weeks is the final test.

### How long does it take for a product to clog pores?

Pore-clogging reactions on human skin can take weeks to months to show up, so a product is not "safe" just because nothing happened in the first few days. This is exactly why changing one product at a time and watching for several weeks matters. If you swap several things at once, you lose the ability to tell which one caused the bumps.

## The Bottom Line

The comedogenic scale isn't useless and it isn't gospel. It's a 1989 rabbit-ear screen that flags ingredients worth watching, and the honest way to use it is as a starting point rather than a verdict: read the full label, know the handful of high-graded names, notice format, change one thing at a time, and let your own skin decide over several weeks. If painful, deep, or scarring acne is the issue, or nothing improves after a few months, that's a dermatologist conversation, not a chart-reading one.

## Why This Happens

Salmon DNA and PDRN are not the same ingredient, and the marketing quietly blurs that line. According to KorMedi (코메디닷컴, June 2025), salmon DNA comes from milt, is high-molecular, and works mostly at the skin's surface for hydration. PDRN is a low-molecular DNA fragment, roughly 50 to 2000 kDa, and it's a different, more expensive material. The cost gap between the two runs about 7 to 10 times. So when a label leans on "PDRN" but the INCI says Sodium DNA, you're often paying a PDRN premium for salmon DNA.

Then there are the numbers on the front of the box. "PDRN 10K," "PDRN 2000," those big figures imply massive potency. But when you look at products that actually disclose amounts, reality is much smaller. Mediheal's Derma 365 PDRN Lifting Mask lists 50 ppb. VT's PDRN Capsule Cream 100 lists 0.5 ppm. Anua's PDRN Bounce Ball Serum lists 108 ppm. Those are tiny, honest numbers. Korean industry experts told KorMedi that claims of "over 10,000 ppm PDRN" are "close to nonsense," partly because one mature salmon yields only about 15ml of milt. The math doesn't support the headline figures.

And regulators noticed. PDRN is not a legally recognized functional (기능성) cosmetic ingredient in Korea. Per MFDS data released by Rep. Seo Young-seok in July 2026, PDRN cosmetic advertising violations climbed from 7 in 2023 to 39 in 2025, plus 41 in the first half of 2026 alone, 106 total. About 76% were drug-misrepresentation cases. Korea isn't banning these products. It's policing the claims. That distinction is the whole story.
